3976: Leading the call for Deng Xiaoping's return puts you with Ye Jianying and rejects the “Two Whatevers”. Wang Dongxing and Hua Guofeng's side will remember.
3977: Speaking by the “Two Whatevers” and following Hua Guofeng repays the favor of that October night. Deng Xiaoping will remember these words once he is back.
3978: Raise your hand and say nothing. You offend neither side and lean on neither, and put your energy into the unions and the workers' and staff congresses. Neither side counts you as theirs.
3979: Leading the discussion in the union system puts you with Deng Xiaoping, openly against Wang Dongxing. Hua Guofeng's side will count you on the other side.
3980: Criticizing it as Wang Dongxing wants keeps you on the “Two Whatevers” path. Union cadres and the workers below may not follow you.
3981: Take no position in Beijing and go back to the mill to do real work, and neither side above can tell where you stand. What to do about Article 14 is left to the people in the shop.
3982: Voting with Ye Jianying's side means breaking with Zhang Chunqiao. He already knows you were the one who reported that Shanghai list.
3983: Not raising your hand means holding to the Chairman's resolution and standing with Zhang Chunqiao. Ye Jianying and the old marshals will decide you are on that side.
3984: Letting Deng Xiaoping return but not join the Standing Committee gives each side a little. No one can find a big fault, and no one will count you as theirs.
3985: Backing Hua Guofeng's plan puts you with those running the economy. Zhang Chunqiao will think you have dropped continuing the revolution, and wages still go unaddressed.
3986: Backing Zhang Chunqiao to shelve the plan puts you on the side of continuing the revolution. Hua Guofeng and Li Xiannian, who runs the economy, will see you as standing in the way.
3987: Cutting big projects to raise workers' wages means both plans must change. Neither Hua Guofeng nor Zhang Chunqiao will be happy. The union people will remember this.
3988: Setting up provincial militia commands apart from the military regions creates a second armed force outside the army. Several of the big military regions will decide you mean to move against them.
3989: Giving way to the army steadies the men with the guns. Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao will say you bowed to the old marshals, and Shanghai's militia will be hard to keep.
3990: Pulling back both army and militia leans on no one, so no one is satisfied. You no longer have a force of your own to command.
3991: Rehabilitating April Fifth overturns the verdict your side set two years ago. Jiang Qing will see it as betrayal. The people in the square will be with you.
3992: Releasing people without rehabilitation keeps the immediate trouble down, but the verdict of two years ago stands. Neither the people in the square nor Jiang Qing will be satisfied.
3993: Doing it the way you did two years ago satisfies Jiang Qing's side, but those arrested are again workers and students, and resentment below toward your faction will run deeper.
3998: Chairman of the CCP Central Committee. Every “Chairman” in the game is him. When the Twelfth Plenum closed in 1968, he told Wang Hongwen, who was attending without a vote, to “stand up and let us have a look”, and in 1972 he proposed bringing Wang Hongwen to Beijing. In July 1974, at a Politburo meeting, he told Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen not to form a “little faction of four”. He died on September 9, 1976. Twenty-seven days later Wang Hongwen and the others were placed under isolation and investigation at Huairen Hall.
3999: Member of the Central Cultural Revolution Group. In early 1967 he and Zhang Chunqiao led the power seizure in Shanghai. When the Shanghai People's Commune was founded on February 5, Zhang Chunqiao became director, and he and Wang Hongwen became deputy directors. He was one of the “little faction of four” Mao Zedong criticized in 1974. On the evening of October 6, 1976, he was placed under isolation and investigation at Huairen Hall.
4000: Mao Zedong's wife and first deputy head of the Central Cultural Revolution Group. After Wang Hongwen came to Beijing, she often sat beside him at Politburo meetings and called him “Little Wang”. In October 1974 she used the Fengqing affair to press Deng Xiaoping to take a position. That night she conferred with Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen, and the next day Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha to complain to Mao Zedong. She was taken from her residence on October 6, 1976. In 1981 the Special Court sentenced her to death with a two-year reprieve.
4003: Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee. The Party Constitution adopted at the Ninth Party Congress named him Mao Zedong's successor, and people then called him “Vice Chairman Lin”. In March 1971 his son Lin Liguo, introduced by Wang Weiguo, had a meal with Wang Hongwen in Shanghai. On September 13 that year the plane carrying Lin Biao crashed in Mongolia, and Wang Hongwen then worked with Xu Shiyou on the Lin Biao case in Shanghai.
4005: Chairman of the People's Republic. In June 1966, while Mao Zedong was away from Beijing, he and Deng Xiaoping ran the Central Committee's front-line work and decided to send work teams into schools and factories. In October 1968 the Twelfth Plenum passed a resolution expelling him from the Party for good. Wang Hongwen attended that meeting without a vote. Liu Shaoqi died in Kaifeng in November 1969.
4006: Army marshal. At the Tenth Party Congress in 1973 he was elected Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee together with Wang Hongwen, ranked after him. After Mao Zedong died he met many people and, with Hua Guofeng and Wang Dongxing, prepared to move against Jiang Qing and the others. On the evening of October 6, 1976, when Wang Hongwen walked into Huairen Hall, the men sitting behind the table inside were Hua Guofeng and Ye Jianying.
4008: Adviser to the Central Cultural Revolution Group. At the Tenth Party Congress in 1973 he was elected Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee at the same time as Wang Hongwen, Ye Jianying and Li Desheng, ranked after Wang Hongwen.
4010: Army general. At the Tenth Party Congress in 1973 he was elected Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee at the same time as Wang Hongwen, Kang Sheng and Ye Jianying, ranked after Wang Hongwen.
4012: Director of the General Office of the Central Committee, in command of the Central Guard Regiment. On the evening of October 5, 1976, he went to Diaoyutai to see Wang Hongwen and told him to come to Huairen Hall at 7:30 the next evening, enter by the east gate and wait first in the East Lounge. That evening Wang Hongwen was arrested at Huairen Hall. Afterward Wang Dongxing sided with Hua Guofeng. He was elected Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee at the Eleventh Party Congress in 1977 and resigned his posts in February 1980.
4014: Founding marshal, former mayor of Shanghai and foreign minister. In 1980 the Special Court charged that in 1968 Wang Hongwen compiled the Collection of Chen Yi's Reactionary Remarks in Shanghai to frame Chen Yi. This was one of the charges against Wang Hongwen.
4016: A Party elder who long ran economic work. At the Central Work Conference in November and December 1978 he raised the Sixty-One Renegades case, Peng Dehuai, the Tiananmen Incident and other questions, and some in the hall applauded. The Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee was held after this conference.
4018: Founding marshal and former defense minister. He was brought down at the 1959 Lushan Conference for criticizing the Great Leap Forward. At the 1978 Central Work Conference, Chen Yun raised his case.
4020: Vice Premier of the State Council, long in charge of finance and the economy. He was elected Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee at the Eleventh Party Congress in August 1977. On one dream path in the game, when the Politburo discusses restoring Deng Xiaoping to work, he says there is too much to do on the economy and they need people.
4022: Founding emperor of the Eastern Han, known as Emperor Guangwu of Han. After the Red Eyebrows were defeated, Liu Penzi, the boy emperor they had set up, surrendered to him. He did not kill Liu Penzi and gave him land to live out his life. In 1973 Zhu Yongjia covered this part when he lectured Wang Hongwen on the Biography of Liu Penzi.
4024: Vice chairman of the Shanghai Federation of Trade Unions. On July 20, 1966, the Municipal Party Committee sent a work team of about 150 people into No. 17 State Cotton Mill, and she led it. The work team the Textile Bureau had sent earlier withdrew. This work team focused the movement on “searching out all ox-demons and snake-spirits” and gave Wang Hongwen no important role.
4026: A worker at the loading machinery plant of the Shanghai Railway Bureau. At the founding rally of the Workers' General Headquarters on November 9, 1966, he went on stage to denounce the private courts at his plant. Halfway through he broke down crying and could not go on, and Xie Pengfei from the same plant went up and finished for him.
4028: Deputy head of the Shanghai Municipal Organization Department. At the founding rally of the Workers' General Headquarters on November 9, 1966, municipal Party secretary Cao Diqiu never came, and the Municipal Party Committee sent him. The crowd demanded that he speak. He said he could not represent the Municipal Party Committee or take a position, and the crowd erupted.
4030: A member of the Shanghai Red Guard organization Bombard Headquarters. From late on November 11 to early on November 12, 1966, Zhang Chunqiao negotiated with worker representatives at the Radio Machinery Plant in Anting. He and Bao Pao of Beijing's Third Headquarters were there as Red Guards, on the side of the workers who had stopped the train.
4032: Head of the Shanghai Municipal Organization Department. When the Scarlet Guards were being organized in November 1966 he expressed support, had Zhang Qi of the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions keep in touch with them, and let them use the federation's offices. After Cao Diqiu declared his signature void on December 25, Chen Pixian said the Scarlet Guards business was the work of Zhang Qi and Yang Shifa, and the Municipal Party Secretariat had not approved it.
4034: Alternate secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. When the Scarlet Guards held their founding rally in People's Square on December 6, 1966, he came and gave a speech of congratulations. During the Shanghai Diesel Incident in August 1967 he, Xu Jingxian and Wang Hongwen set up a command post in a factory nearby. According to Li Xun, he opposed smashing the Liansi and told Wang Hongwen to ask Zhang Chunqiao first. Huang Jinhai records him as chairing the meeting on Kangping Road on the night of October 12, 1976.
4036: A man from Scarlet Guards headquarters. On the morning of December 23, 1966, he ran into Wang Hongwen, Pan Guoping and others in the canteen of the Glass Machinery Plant and invited the Workers' General Headquarters to the Scarlet Guards' rally in People's Square that afternoon. After the rally that day, Cao Diqiu signed the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands.
4038: A worker at No. 31 State Cotton Mill and a member of the Workers' General Headquarters. When the Scarlet Guards held their rally in People's Square on December 23, 1966, Wang Hongwen and Pan Guoping both said they could not go and sent him to represent WGHQ. He was invited onto the rostrum. After the rally broke up that day, Cao Diqiu signed the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands.
4040: A member of the Workers' General Headquarters. On the evening of December 29, 1966, he rode with Wang Hongwen, Pan Guoping and Huang Jinhai in the headquarters car to Kangping Road to see what was happening. The car stalled outside the Hengshan Hotel. Wang Hongwen and the others were afraid of being recognized and stayed in the car. He got out and asked Scarlet Guards for help, and they pushed the car until it started.
4042: Deputy commander of the Qinghai Provincial Military District. On January 23, 1967, he put commander Liu Xianquan, who backed the rebel group “August 18”, under house arrest and seized power in the military district. On February 23 troops surrounded the Qinghai Daily and opened fire, killing 169 people. On March 24 Zhou Enlai ordered him taken away, and the Center labeled it a counterrevolutionary coup.
4044: A member of the headquarters staff of the Workers' General Headquarters. In February 1967 he and Fan Zuodong put up a notice at headquarters saying any Standing Committee member who did not come to work there for three days would be struck off. It was aimed at Wang Hongwen and Pan Guoping, who were often away. On February 25 Wang Hongwen dealt with Fan Zuodong, and Huang Wenhai was also locked up for more than half a year.
4046: A cadre in the office of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. On August 3, 1967, at a meeting on the Shanghai Diesel Liansi held at “888”, the Support-the-Left Office of the Garrison Command, people from the Workers' General Headquarters said the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee was too soft. He said men and vehicles could only be dispatched by the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee, and the two sides quarreled.
4048: One of the leaders of the Workers' General Headquarters. According to Li Xun, on the evening of December 29, 1966, he and Wang Hongwen went to the Second Regiment's base and divided up with Geng Jinzhang the job of dealing with the Scarlet Guards on Kangping Road. During the Shanghai Diesel Incident on August 4, 1967, he was at the command post, and the two fountain pens in his breast pocket were snapped by something thrown from a rooftop.
4050: A member of the Workers' General Headquarters. In the Shanghai Diesel Incident of August 4, 1967, he was hit in the stomach by something thrown from the roof. After the fighting ended he searched the whole plant and reported over the walkie-talkie that no one was dead. His recollections are one of Li Xun's sources for how Wang Hongwen acted at Shanghai Diesel.
4052: One of the leaders of the Workers' General Headquarters. On August 3, 1967, he took part in the “888” meeting on the Shanghai Diesel Liansi. Zhang Chunqiao's telephone instructions of July 13 are recorded in Ye Changming's Work Notes. After 1976 his name was on the Shanghai list the special case group wanted Wang Hongwen to inform on.
4054: One of the leaders of the Workers' General Headquarters. When the two factions at Shanghai Diesel clashed in 1967, Wang Hongwen took him on his motorcycle to the plant gate. On the night of January 29, 1967, when Red Guards bombarded Zhang Chunqiao, he said at Zhang's residence that the workers would act. At the meeting on Kangping Road on the night of October 12, 1976, he proposed sinking a 10,000-ton ship in the Huangpu River to close it and blocking the airport runways with trucks, and he sat in the doorway so no one could leave.
4056: A man from the Shanghai Light Industry Bureau and one of Wang Hongwen's trusted lieutenants. Xu Shiyou once introduced him to a prospective wife. Investigation materials from 1977 say Wang Hongwen colluded with him to take large quantities of color TVs, cameras, premium cigarettes and other products from the Light Industry Bureau. These are the investigators' allegations, and the amounts have not been independently verified.
4058: The official then in charge of Tsinghua University. At the Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius rally on January 25, 1974, he and Xie Jingyi criticized the back door.
4060: Formerly Mao Zedong's confidential secretary, then working at Tsinghua University. At the Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius rally on January 25, 1974, she and Chi Qun criticized the back door.
4062: Zhejiang provincial Party secretary. In February 1974 rebels in Hangzhou set up a militia command, Weng Senhe became deputy head of the provincial Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius leading group, and Tan Qilong was pushed aside. On March 16 Wang Hongwen phoned him.
4064: A Ministry of Transport cadre sent to sail with the Fengqing. When the Fengqing returned to Shanghai from its ocean voyage in 1974, he and Gu Wenguang refused to criticize the State Council and the Ministry of Transport. They were held in Shanghai for struggle sessions and told they could not go back to Beijing until they had criticized thoroughly.
4066: A Ministry of Transport cadre sent to sail with the Fengqing. When the Fengqing returned to Shanghai from its ocean voyage in 1974, he and Li Guotang refused to criticize the State Council and the Ministry of Transport. They were held in Shanghai for struggle sessions and told they could not go back to Beijing until they had criticized thoroughly.
4068: A man from Liuzhou Iron and Steel. According to Yang Jisheng's The World Turned Upside Down, he was connected to the 1968 killings in Guangxi. He later became deputy Party secretary of Liuzhou Iron and Steel and vice chairman of the Guangxi Federation of Trade Unions. In the game he appears only on one dream path, as a name on the list of union cadres Guangxi sent up.
4070: Head of the Shanghai Militia Command. At the meeting on Kangping Road on the night of October 12, 1976, he opposed sending militia to seize the radio station, saying that calling out the militia needed an order from the Municipal Party Committee and would take a day. After the meeting he wired the district militias not to act on their own. He later said his idea was to stall.
4072: One of Shanghai's leading cadres. According to Li Xun, he chaired the meeting on Kangping Road on the night of October 12, 1976, asking each person present for their position one by one. Huang Jinhai's memoir records the chair as Wang Shaoyong. The game follows Li Xun.
4074: Navy commander. After October 1976 the Center sent him, Ni Zhifu and Peng Chong to take charge in Shanghai.
4076: A Beijing worker and national model worker who joined the Politburo after the Tenth Party Congress in 1973. After October 1976 the Center sent him, Su Zhenhua and Peng Chong to take charge in Shanghai. At the Ninth National Congress of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions in October 1978 he was elected its chairman.
4078: Air force commander from Lin Biao's camp. He was at the meeting Lin Liguo called on Yueyang Road in Shanghai on March 31, 1971. Later he was held in the same courtyard at Qincheng as Qiu Huizuo and Wang Hongwen. According to the Memoirs of Qiu Huizuo, he joked about Wang Hongwen's treatment during exercise time.
4080: Mao Zedong's nephew and his liaison officer in 1976. After Mao Zedong died, at the Politburo meeting of September 29, Jiang Qing wanted him to stay in Beijing to sort Mao Zedong's papers, and Hua Guofeng and Ye Jianying wanted him back in Liaoning. They argued late into the night. He was taken from his residence on the evening of October 6.
4082: A scholar of the Cultural Revolution in Shanghai and author of The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion, a book of more than 1,600 pages. Li Xun was a middle school student in Shanghai at the time and was on the conservative side. Many scenes and source notes in the game draw on this book and on Li Xun's articles.
4087: At 6:30 on the morning of November 10, 1966, you came back to work at the security section of No. 17 State Cotton Mill, and you stayed until the mill was restructured in the 1990s. In your fifties you took a buyout of your years of service and went home. At the founding rally you told everyone to go home, but that night more than 2,000 people boarded trains at North Station anyway and stopped at Anting. On the 13th Zhang Chunqiao signed at Culture Square, and the man beside him was Pan Guoping. Kangping Road, the January Storm and Shanghai Diesel all happened as before. In October 1976 three people were arrested at Huairen Hall, and your name was not among those read over the shop loudspeaker. In the 1977 investigation at the mill, someone dug up your name from the Culture Square sign-in, and you wrote three self-criticisms.
4088: In December 1966 you left the hospital in Jiading County and went back to the security section at No. 17 State Cotton Mill. On the platform at Anting you had said those harsh words in front of everyone. The crowd surged toward you, and you fell off the edge of the platform and hit the back of your head on the gravel of the railbed. Your left leg went into a cast. On November 13 Zhang Chunqiao signed to recognize the Workers' General Headquarters, and the man beside him was Pan Guoping. Afterward Kangping Road, the January Storm and the Shanghai Diesel Liansi all happened, every one of them, and your name was missing from every list. In October 1976 you listened to the broadcast in the security section and counted the “Gang of Four”. There were only three. In the 1990s the mill cut spindles, and you retired in your fifties.
4089: This playthrough stops at No. 17 State Cotton Mill in January 1967. You are the head of the Workers' General Headquarters, and at the end of the list in the Extra-Urgent Order is Master Qian, whom you added. He was taken away on January 2 and held in the yarn storeroom behind the fine-spinning shop. On the fifth night someone beat his legs with a carrying pole. On the tenth day the Public Security Bureau came and said he was not on the city's list, and only then was he let go. His left leg never straightened again. He was later moved to guard the mill gate, and he guarded it until the mill cut spindles in 1994. History went on as before. You still went to Beijing, still became Vice Chairman, still were arrested at Huairen Hall. In the 1977 investigation he came on crutches to testify, and the entry under your name in the dossier reads “retaliated out of personal grudge, causing disability”.
4090: In January 1967 you lay in a Shanghai hospital with a fractured skull and three broken ribs. On the last day of 1966 you had led men to Kunshan yourself to stop the Scarlet Guards, and by the railway someone recognized you. You heard the January 6 rally in People's Square over the radio from your hospital bed. Pan Guoping and Huang Jinhai read the denunciation on stage. After you left the hospital you ranked seventh or eighth in the Workers' General Headquarters. You later served as vice chairman of a district revolutionary committee. After 1976 you were investigated for two years, found to have made serious mistakes, and sent back to the mill to work. The Scarlet Guard in the next bed had also been hurt at Kunshan. The two of you didn't speak for a month. The day he left, his wife filled the thermos at your bedside on her way out.
4091: On February 5, 1967, you sat in the security section of No. 17 State Cotton Mill, listening to the list read out at People's Square. You were not on it. On the night of January 11 you didn't wait for Zhang Chunqiao. You took 300 men into the Municipal Party Committee building and sealed it with Workers' General Headquarters seals. Other organizations said you were keeping it all for yourself, and Xu Jingxian phoned to say Zhang Chunqiao considered it grabbing power. Three days later WGHQ met without you, suspended you from all posts and put Huang Jinhai in charge. After that you spent ten years in the security section. In 1977 the investigation group found the page in your dossier, “dismissed by the Workers' General Headquarters, January 1967”, and wrote “not a serious problem” for you.
4092: In March 1967 the Shanghai People's Commune still had its name, and you lost the election at No. 17 State Cotton Mill. The day of the renaming you said no, and Zhang Chunqiao agreed to try it for a month first. The mills cut ballots from the backs of cigarette packs. No. 17 Mill elected an old loom tender in her fifties, and you got about sixty votes fewer. The Second Regiment won majorities in a dozen or so mills. Output in March fell well below February. A staff officer from the Garrison Command sat in the last row at Commune meetings taking notes. At the end of March, Beijing called and told you to come.
